x.name: alphaXiv
x.bio: High fidelity research

tweets.text:
“Automated Researchers Can Reliably Mitigate Alignment Failures”

This paper demonstrates that AI researchers can autonomously discover and test methods for making other AI models safer across 10 different alignment failures.

From searching the literature and proposing post-training methods to training and evaluating models, the this system run the full research loop themselves. 

They repeatedly improve failures like deception, jailbreaks, and reward hacking, with the fixes generalizing to unseen evaluations and models up to 4.7x larger.

https://t.co/Gic5CeafQM

“LeVJEPA: Efficient & Scalable Video Pretraining without the Heuristics”

This paper makes video pretraining simpler and cheaper by replacing the target encoder, predictor, stop-gradient, and reconstruction machinery with a single encoder trained using invariance + SIGReg.

From randomly dropping 95% of video tokens, preventing representation collapse, all the way to learning causal frame representations, LeVJEPA matches or beats V-JEPA 2 with 5.6–20.8x less compute while preserving appearance and motion understanding.

https://t.co/ntXITxFm3Z

"TTPO: Test-Time Policy Optimization"

This paper shows how an LLM can keep improving while solving problems, even when there's no ground truth.

The idea is that the model samples many solutions and uses the majority answer as a rough signal. But instead of fully trusting that majority, TTPO learns from it carefully by strengthening solutions that agree, penalizing likely-wrong solutions that disagree, and only updating the tokens that actually look uncertain or wrong.

https://t.co/Nqs94DIoYe

x.name: Madhu Guru
x.bio: Sr Director, AI at Meta; Prev: Google - Led Gemini, Veo, Nano Banana.

tweets.text:
AI product building has a ~3-month playbook half-life. Here’s how to adapt.

Most trad product teams are built to discover a playbook and then milk it for the next 5 years.

However in the AI labs, we consciously throw away playbooks every few months cos we start seeing diminishing returns.

Here’s what you can do as an AI builder:

Focus on defining a set of meta-principles for 
1/ how you continuously learn what the market wants today and what it might want in 3 months
2/ how you execute with extreme urgency

The specifics of 1 and 2 will vary based on your domain and product type.
Build a team that learns and adapts at that pace. 

Legacy teams are optimized for playbook milking.

AI teams need to be optimized for inventing.

x.name: Aaron Levie
x.bio: ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI

tweets.text:
The average strongly held belief these days in AI has a half life of 6 months at best. Here are just a few the industry has cycled through and probably has no consensus on at the moment:

* OSS is too far behind to catch up 

* The labs can’t be profitable at scale

* All software will be replaced by agents

* You can’t build moats on top of models

* Cheaper models will mean less compute

* You don’t need evals

* RAG is dead 

* AI will decimate engineering jobs

* Prompting won’t matter in the future 

* We’ve hit a training wall

* Frontier models are too dangerous to release 

…and dozens and dozens more. The key here is to remain flexible in your thinking because we’re going to be in a constant state of change for a while.

Source: https://t.co/LY26WSu0iL

5 human records were beaten at the World Humanoid Robot Games in China that ended a few days ago, fully autonomously!

Across 51 events, two robot makers had the strongest showing:
— Agibot, and their wheeled Genie G2 (~$140k) and Agilink OmniHand Ultra (~$61k), which crushed the task based events
— X-Humanoid, and their Tiangong Ultra (~$41k), which crushed athletics

Unitree ($37B), which stole the show last year and popped in its IPO this year, scaled back the night of the preliminaries with a poor showing. In a big change from last year, most events required full autonomy with only teleop / remote allowed for certain task based events.

This is incredible progress in just 1 year in humanoid robotics. A year ago the best 100m was 21.5s. China continues to demonstrate its lead. They ship 86-97% of the world's humanoid robots. We are close to superhuman physicality and getting there on autonomy in certain domains. And there's a long way to go: the bots could only lift 16kg in the weightlifting event. And yes, they'd occasionally blow up.

This is the worst the humanoids will ever get.
